name: Kanyam
tagline: Open tea slopes on the Mechi Highway, and sunrise at Antu Danda
meta_description: Kanyam, Ilam: Nepal's best-known open tea garden at about 1,570 m, with Antu Danda sunrise nearby. How to reach, when to go and where to stay.
summary: Kanyam is a tea garden and roadside settlement at about 1,570 m in Suryodaya municipality, Ilam district. Its open, rolling slopes are the most photographed tea scene in Nepal. Pair it with sunrise at Antu Danda and the market towns of Fikkal and Pashupatinagar, all within an hour or so.
intro: Kanyam sits right on the Mechi Highway, the road that climbs from the Terai to Ilam. Unlike the steep, terraced gardens around Ilam bazaar, the slopes here are broad and rounded, with tea clipped close over the hilltops and a few shade trees standing alone. On weekends and holidays the place is full of families from Jhapa, Morang and across the border, posing for photographs between the rows and buying snacks at the stalls by the road.

On a weekday morning it is a different place. Pickers work the rows, mist rolls in from the south, and you can walk for an hour along the garden paths and see more people working than visiting. The garden has small tea stalls and snack shops by the road, and a factory nearby processes the leaf. At about 1,570 m the air is cool, and in spring and autumn the light at either end of the day is soft and low.

Most travellers come for an hour on the way to Ilam. We suggest a night nearby instead, so you can see the garden early and late in the day, when it is empty, and drive to Antu Danda for sunrise over the plains and the Kanchenjunga range. Add a morning in the market towns of Fikkal and Pashupatinagar, and Kanyam becomes a full and easy day in the tea hills rather than a quick photo stop.

story.title: A garden on the old road to Ilam
paras: Before the Mechi Highway, the hills between the Terai and Ilam were reached on foot along porter trails, with goods carried up from the plains in baskets and cardamom and ginger carried down. The road, built and improved over several decades, brought trucks, buses and tea factories to places like Kanyam and Fikkal, and turned small hill hamlets into roadside markets. Kanyam's open garden became a stop simply because it lay beside the road and looked the way people imagine tea country should.

Today Kanyam belongs to Suryodaya municipality, with its offices in Fikkal bazaar just down the road. The garden employs pickers from the surrounding villages, many of them women from Rai, Limbu, Tamang and other hill families, who walk in each morning during the plucking season. Leaf goes to a nearby factory for processing, and the garden's name appears on packets sold in the bazaars. Around the estate, smallholders grow their own tea and sell green leaf to factories, as across much of Ilam.

Tourism here is mostly domestic. Nepali and Indian families arrive by bus and jeep for photographs and picnics, which is why you will find snack stalls and photo spots by the road, and why the place feels like a fairground on a holiday afternoon. Walk five minutes into the rows and the crowd thins quickly. For the people who live here, visitors are a useful extra income on top of tea, dairy and farming, and many families now run small lodges and homestays.

people: The villages around Kanyam and Fikkal are mixed: Limbu and Rai families with the oldest roots, Brahmin, Chhetri, Tamang, Magar and Newar households who came with farming and trade, and a few Lepcha families in the wider district. Tea plucking, dairy, broom grass and vegetable farming are the main work, along with shops and lodges on the highway. Nepali is the common language.

untold.fact: Kanyam is not a separate municipality. It lies within Suryodaya municipality of Ilam district, whose administrative centre is the market town of Fikkal a short drive away.
Nepal's orthodox tea follows four flushes: first flush from about the fourth week of March, second flush from May, a monsoon flush, and an autumn flush in October and November.
The Mechi Highway that passes Kanyam climbs about 74 km from the East–West Highway in Jhapa to Ilam bazaar, linking the tea hills with the Terai.

taste.name: Ilam green tea
taste.text: Kanyam's roadside stalls serve green tea and sweet milk tea made from local leaf, with pakoda and noodles on the side. For a better cup, ask your lodge to brew loose orthodox green or first-flush tea, and drink it on the porch as the mist comes in.

facts: Open tea slopes, Antu Danda sunrise

highlights.title: The open slopes of Kanyam
highlights.text: Rounded hills of clipped tea with single shade trees, right beside the highway. Walk the paths away from the road for the quiet rows and wide views south toward the Terai haze and north to Ilam's ridges.

highlights.title: Sunrise at Antu Danda
highlights.text: A hilltop at about 2,300 m near the Indian border, roughly an hour or so by jeep from Kanyam. On clear mornings you see the sun come up over the plains and catch first light on the Kanchenjunga range to the north.

highlights.title: Pickers at work
highlights.text: From late March to November, pickers move through the rows with doko baskets on their backs. Early morning is the best time to see them. Ask first before taking photographs, and keep to the paths.

highlights.title: Fikkal and Pashupatinagar markets
highlights.text: Fikkal is the municipal centre and a busy highway bazaar. Pashupatinagar, on the Indian border, has a market where you find cheese, chhurpi, oranges in winter and tea from small growers, with buyers from both sides of the border.

highlights.title: A night in the tea hills
highlights.text: Staying a night nearby lets you see the garden empty at dawn and dusk, the hours most day visitors miss. Several simple lodges and homestays operate around Kanyam and Fikkal, and the evenings are quiet and cool.

how_to_reach.text: Kanyam is on the Mechi Highway, roughly 2–2.5 hours by car from Bhadrapur airport and about 35 km (around 1–1.5 hours) from Ilam bazaar. Local buses and shared jeeps between the Terai and Ilam stop at Kanyam. Road times stretch in the monsoon; check current status before you travel.
The nearest airport is Bhadrapur in Jhapa, with flights of about 45–50 minutes from Kathmandu. From the airport we drive via Birtamod or Charali and up the Mechi Highway to Kanyam.

where_to_stay: Kanyam and nearby Fikkal have simple lodges, small hotels and homestays, mostly run by local families and aimed at domestic visitors. Rooms are basic and clean; expect shared or simple private bathrooms and hot water by geyser or bucket. For more choice, stay in Ilam bazaar and drive to Kanyam for the day, or base yourself in Fikkal for an early start to Antu Danda. Book ahead for Nepali holidays and Saturdays.
tips: Come early in the morning or late afternoon; from late morning on weekends the garden fills with day visitors.
Ask before photographing pickers, and never pull leaves for a picture.
For Antu Danda, leave Kanyam before 5 am in autumn and winter to reach the top before sunrise.
Carry a light rain jacket in every season; mist and drizzle arrive fast on these slopes.
Foreign nationals other than Indians should not cross the border at Pashupatinagar without the correct entry permissions for India.

experiences.title: Kanyam tea garden walk with a local guide
experiences.summary: An early walk through Kanyam's open garden before the day crowd arrives, with a local guide who knows the pickers, the plucking calendar and the paths that lead away from the road to the quiet hilltops.
body: We start at the roadside stalls just after sunrise and walk up into the rows. Kanyam's slopes are wide and gentle, so the walk is easy and the views open quickly: Ilam's ridges to the north, the plains to the south when the air is clear, and shade trees standing alone on the green. Paths wind along the tops of the hills and down into small hollows, and our guide chooses a loop that avoids the busiest photo spots by the road.

Our guide grew up in the area and explains how the garden works through the year: pruning in winter, first flush from late March, the heavy monsoon flush, and the autumn picking. If pickers are working nearby, we stop to talk, with their permission, about pay, hours and the doko baskets they carry. You learn why the bushes are kept at waist height, and how the leaf is weighed at the end of each shift before going to the factory.

The walk ends back at the road with a cup of tea from one of the stalls, usually sweet milk tea or a simple green. If you are staying the night, we come back in the late afternoon when the light turns gold and most visitors have left, and walk a different loop. The two walks together show you the garden at its quietest and most photogenic, and give you time to sit and watch the mist come and go.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Kanyam tea garden?
faqs.a: On our recent visits there was no formal entry ticket to walk the main paths in Kanyam's garden, though local rules can change. Keep to the paths, do not pick leaves and respect any areas marked off. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Kanyam?
faqs.a: An hour is enough for photographs on the way to Ilam. For a proper walk away from the road, allow two to three hours. We suggest staying one night nearby so you can see the garden at dawn and dusk, when it is empty and the light is best.

faqs.q: Is the Kanyam walk suitable for children and older travellers?
faqs.a: Yes. The slopes are gentle and the paths short, at about 1,570 m, so there is no altitude concern for most people. Some paths are steep in short sections and slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip, and we keep the pace slow with plenty of stops.

experiences.title: Sunrise at Antu Danda
experiences.summary: A pre-dawn jeep ride from Kanyam or Fikkal to Antu Danda, a ridge top at about 2,300 m on the Nepal–India border, to watch the sun rise over the plains and light the Kanchenjunga range.
body: We leave in the dark, usually between 4 and 5 am depending on the season, and drive up through tea and forest to the base of Antu Danda. From the road it is a short, steep walk to the top, where a viewing area looks east and north. Bring a head torch for the path and a warm layer for the wait; you will be standing still in the cold for half an hour or more before the light comes.

On clear mornings, mostly from October to February, the sun comes up over the plains and the haze below, and a few minutes later the snow on the Kanchenjunga range to the north turns pink, then white. In spring the view is often hazier, but the rhododendrons on the slopes make up for it. Local families come up on holidays, so expect company at sunrise, and on festival days a cheerful crowd.

We drink tea at the stalls near the top while the light changes, and our guide points out the plains of Jhapa, the hills of Darjeeling across the border and the ridges leading north toward Sandakpur. Once the sun is up, we walk down and drive back for breakfast at Kanyam, or carry on toward Ilam. The whole outing takes about four hours, leaving the rest of the day free.

faqs.q: Can you see Kanchenjunga from Antu Danda?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear mornings the Kanchenjunga range is visible to the north from Antu Danda. October to February gives the best odds, especially after a night of rain has cleared the air. In spring haze often hides the peaks, and in the monsoon months cloud usually covers them completely.

faqs.q: How far is Antu Danda from Kanyam?
faqs.a: Antu Danda is roughly an hour or a little more by jeep from Kanyam or Fikkal, followed by a short steep walk to the top. Road conditions vary, so we allow extra time and leave early to reach the top before sunrise. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How cold is Antu Danda at sunrise?
faqs.a: In winter it can be near freezing before dawn at about 2,300 m, and windy. Bring a down jacket or fleece, hat and gloves from November to February. In autumn and spring a warm layer is still needed for the first hour.

experiences.title: Fikkal and Pashupatinagar market morning
experiences.summary: A morning in the two market towns near Kanyam: Fikkal, the highway bazaar and municipal centre, and Pashupatinagar on the Indian border, with stalls of cheese, chhurpi, tea, oranges and hill produce bought by traders from both countries.
body: Fikkal is where the villages around Kanyam do their shopping: cloth, tools, phone credit and groceries along the Mechi Highway. It is a working bazaar rather than a sight, and a good place to see the hill economy up close, from farmers selling vegetables to porters loading jeeps. We stop for tea and sel roti, the ring-shaped fried rice bread, and walk the main street with our guide, who knows many of the shopkeepers.

Pashupatinagar lies a short drive east on the border with Darjeeling district in India. The market here draws buyers from both sides, and you will hear Nepali spoken by everyone, whichever side they come from. Look for local cheese and hard chhurpi, tea from small growers, cardamom, ginger and, in winter, piles of oranges from the hill farms. Prices are lower than in Kathmandu, and bargaining is polite and light.

Nepali and Indian citizens cross here freely; other nationalities should stay on the Nepal side unless they hold the correct entry permissions for India, and should not assume this crossing handles foreign immigration. Our guide helps with prices and introductions, and makes sure you know where the border line runs. Then we drive back to Kanyam for lunch or on to Ilam, with your bag a little heavier than when you started.

faqs.q: Can foreigners cross into India at Pashupatinagar?
faqs.a: Nepali and Indian citizens cross freely here. Other nationals need the correct Indian visa or entry permissions and should check whether this crossing is open to them for immigration formalities; often it is not. Stay on the Nepal side unless your papers are confirmed. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What should I buy in Pashupatinagar?
faqs.a: Look for loose orthodox tea from small growers, hard chhurpi cheese, cardamom, akabare chilli pickle and, from about November to February, oranges from the hill farms. Prices are lower than in Kathmandu. Carry Nepali rupees in small notes, and ask our guide before agreeing a price.

faqs.q: When are the markets busiest?
faqs.a: Mornings are busiest, and weekends and the days before major festivals such as Dashain and Tihar are crowded, with traffic jams at the border. Weekday mornings are calmer and better for talking with sellers and taking photographs without the crush.

experiences.title: Golden hour and a homestay night in Kanyam
experiences.summary: Stay when the day visitors leave: a late-afternoon walk in the empty garden, dinner with a local family or at a simple lodge, and a quiet night in the tea hills before an early start.
body: Most visitors to Kanyam stop for an hour and drive on. By about 4 pm the buses have gone and the garden belongs to the pickers walking home and the people who live here. This is the time to walk the rows again, with low sun across the clipped tea and long shadows from the shade trees. On many evenings the mist arrives just after sunset, filling the hollows and leaving the hilltops above it.

We book you into a simple lodge or homestay in Kanyam or nearby. Dinner is home-style: rice, dal, seasonal greens, a pickle, perhaps chicken or pork, and milk tea. If you stay with a family, you eat with them in the kitchen and can ask about their work in tea and farming. Evenings are quiet, with little to do after dark but talk and sleep, and the mist often rolls in after dark.

The night sets you up for Antu Danda at sunrise or an early, empty walk in the garden. It suits couples, photographers and anyone who wants a slow day between Ilam and the plains. In the morning, we either drive up to Antu Danda before dawn or walk the rows at first light, then have breakfast and continue to Ilam, Bhadrapur or the market towns of Fikkal and Pashupatinagar.

faqs.q: Are there hotels at Kanyam?
faqs.a: Yes, there are simple lodges, small hotels and homestays at Kanyam and in nearby Fikkal, run mostly by local families. Rooms are basic and clean. For more choice, stay in Ilam bazaar and visit Kanyam on a day trip, about an hour or so away.

faqs.q: Is Kanyam a good place for a honeymoon?
faqs.a: It is popular with Nepali and Indian couples for its open tea slopes and cool air. Expect simple lodges rather than resorts. For a quiet stay, come on weekdays, walk the garden at dawn and dusk, and add Antu Danda at sunrise.

faqs.q: What is the weather like at Kanyam in the evening?
faqs.a: At about 1,570 m, evenings are cool in spring and autumn and cold in December to February, often with mist and dew. Bring a fleece or warm jacket and a hat. In the monsoon it is damp and cloudy most evenings, and rooms can feel humid.

faqs.q: Where is Kanyam?
faqs.a: Kanyam is in Suryodaya municipality, Ilam district, Koshi Province, in far eastern Nepal. It lies on the Mechi Highway between the Terai and Ilam bazaar, at about 1,570 m, close to the Indian border with Darjeeling district. Fikkal, the municipal centre, is a short drive away.

faqs.q: How do I get to Kanyam from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Fly from Kathmandu to Bhadrapur (about 45–50 minutes), then drive roughly 2–2.5 hours up the Mechi Highway. By road the whole trip from Kathmandu takes about 13–15 hours by bus. Flight schedules and road conditions change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kanyam?
faqs.a: October to December for clear air, autumn plucking and views of the Kanchenjunga range from Antu Danda. March to May for first and second flush and greener slopes, with more haze. Monsoon (June to September) brings cloud, rain and leeches but very lush tea.

faqs.q: Is Kanyam the same as Ilam?
faqs.a: Kanyam is in Ilam district but is not Ilam town. Ilam bazaar, the district headquarters, is about 35 km away along the Mechi Highway. Most people visit both: Kanyam for the open garden and Antu Danda, Ilam for the old estate, tea shops and Mai Pokhari.

faqs.q: How much time do I need at Kanyam?
faqs.a: An hour for a stop on the way to Ilam, a half day for a proper walk, or one night if you want sunrise at Antu Danda and an empty garden at dawn. Many travellers combine Kanyam and Ilam in three nights.

faqs.q: What is Antu Danda?
faqs.a: Antu Danda, also called Shree Antu, is a ridge-top viewpoint at about 2,300 m near Kanyam and Fikkal, right on the Nepal–India border. It is known for sunrise over the plains and, on clear mornings, a view of the Kanchenjunga range.

faqs.q: Can I buy tea at Kanyam?
faqs.a: Yes. Roadside stalls and shops sell packets from local factories and small growers. For a wider choice and side-by-side tastings, the shops in Ilam bazaar are better. Ask for a price per 100 grams, taste before buying where you can, and compare two or three sellers.

faqs.q: Is Kanyam crowded?
faqs.a: On Saturdays, public holidays and during Dashain and Tihar, yes: families from the Terai and India arrive by the busload from mid-morning, and the roadside can be jammed. On weekday mornings and late afternoons it is quiet. Plan your visit around those hours.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kanyam?
faqs.a: No permit is needed to visit Kanyam, Fikkal or Antu Danda; this is not a protected or restricted area. Carry your passport, as hotels record foreign guests. Do not cross into India at the nearby border unless you hold the correct papers for that crossing.
